title: Quadrilaterals and Regular Polygons
summary: Learn the properties of every special quadrilateral, how they fit into a hierarchy, and why a regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order n.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Identify and describe the **hierarchy of quadrilaterals**: know the properties of each special quadrilateral and explain which shapes are special types of other shapes (for example, every square is a rectangle). (8Gg.01)
Understand that for a **regular polygon**, the number of sides = the number of lines of symmetry = the order of rotational symmetry. (8Gg.09)
This means: use sides, angles, parallel lines, diagonals and symmetry to name and sort quadrilaterals, and use the 'n sides → n lines → order n' rule for regular polygons.

blocks.text: 1. Key words

items: quadrilateral
شكل رباعي — a 2D shape with 4 straight sides
parallel
متوازي — lines that never meet; they stay the same distance apart (marked with arrows ›)
perpendicular
عمودي — lines that meet at a right angle (90°)
adjacent sides
أضلاع متجاورة — sides that are next to each other (they share a vertex)
opposite sides
أضلاع متقابلة — sides that face each other (they do not touch)
diagonal
قطر — a straight line joining two opposite vertices
bisect
ينصف — cut into two equal parts
hierarchy
تسلسل هرمي — an order from general (at the top) to special (at the bottom)
regular polygon
مضلع منتظم — all sides equal AND all angles equal
line of symmetry
محور تماثل — a mirror line: one half is the reflection of the other
order of rotational symmetry
رتبة التماثل الدوراني — how many times a shape fits onto itself in one full turn

blocks.text: 2. The special quadrilaterals
Diagrams use marks to show properties. **Dashes** (|, ||) on sides mean those sides are equal. **Arrows** (›, ››) mean those sides are parallel. A small **square** in a corner means a right angle.

blocks.text: An **isosceles trapezium** is a trapezium whose two non-parallel sides are equal. It has 1 line of symmetry and equal diagonals.

blocks.title: Diagonals are the quickest test
items: Diagonals **equal** and **bisect each other** → rectangle (or square).
Diagonals **bisect each other at 90°** → rhombus (or square).
Diagonals **cross at 90°** but only **one** is cut in half → kite.
Diagonals **bisect each other** only → parallelogram.

blocks.text: 3. The hierarchy of quadrilaterals

A **hierarchy** puts the most general shape at the top and the most special shape at the bottom. A shape lower down has **all the properties** of every shape it is joined to above it, **plus extra ones**. So it is a special type of each of them.

blocks.caption: The hierarchy of quadrilaterals. Follow the arrows upwards: a square is a rectangle and a rhombus; a rhombus is a parallelogram and a kite; a parallelogram is a trapezium.

items: A **square** is a special **rectangle** (a rectangle with 4 equal sides).
A **square** is a special **rhombus** (a rhombus with right angles).
A **rectangle** and a **rhombus** are both special **parallelograms**.
A **rhombus** is a special **kite** (both pairs of adjacent sides are equal, so all 4 sides are equal).
A **parallelogram** is a special **trapezium** (it has two pairs of parallel sides, so it certainly has at least one).
Every one of them is a **quadrilateral**.

blocks.text: **Reading the hierarchy the other way does NOT work.** 'Every square is a rectangle' is true, but 'every rectangle is a square' is false: most rectangles have two long and two short sides. To show that a statement like this is false, give **one counter-example** (one shape that breaks it).

blocks.title: A note about the word 'trapezium'
blocks.text: In the hierarchy we use the definition **'at least one pair of parallel sides'**, so a parallelogram counts as a special trapezium. Some books say 'exactly one pair'. In a hierarchy question, always place the parallelogram under the trapezium, as in the diagram above.

blocks.title: الفكرة الأساسية بالعربي
blocks.text: الشكل اللي تحت في الشجرة بياخد كل خواص الشكل اللي فوقه وزيادة. يعني المربع مستطيل (لأن زواياه قائمة) والمربع معين (لأن أضلاعه متساوية). لكن العكس مش صح: مش كل مستطيل مربع. ولو عايز تثبت إن جملة غلط، هات مثال واحد بس يكسرها (counter-example).
4. How to identify a quadrilateral, step by step

items: **Count the pairs of parallel sides** (look for arrows, or check gradients on a grid). 0 pairs → kite or a general quadrilateral; 1 pair → trapezium; 2 pairs → parallelogram family.
**Check the sides**: all equal? opposite equal? adjacent pairs equal?
**Check the angles**: right angles? opposite angles equal?
**Check the diagonals** if they are given: equal? cross at 90°? bisect each other?
**Choose the most special name** that fits all the facts, then check upwards in the hierarchy: the shape is also every shape above it.

blocks.text: **On a coordinate grid**, compare the 'steps' along each side (across and up). Two sides with the same step (for example 1 right, 3 up) are **parallel and equal**. Count squares to compare horizontal and vertical lengths. Do not measure a slanted length by counting squares along it.
5. Symmetry of regular polygons
A **regular polygon** has **all sides equal and all angles equal**. For every regular polygon:

blocks.title: The rule (8Gg.09)
blocks.text: **number of sides = number of lines of symmetry = order of rotational symmetry.** A regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order n. The smallest turn that fits it back onto itself is **360° ÷ n**.

blocks.caption: Every regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry (dashed) and rotational symmetry of order n.

blocks.text: **Where are the lines?** If n is **odd** (triangle, pentagon, heptagon…), each line goes from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. If n is **even** (square, hexagon, octagon…), half of the lines join opposite vertices and half join the midpoints of opposite sides.

blocks.text: **The rule only works for regular polygons.** Compare the quadrilaterals:

Order 1 means the shape only fits onto itself after a **full** turn, so it has **no** rotational symmetry. A shape with all sides equal is **not** always regular: the hexagon below has 6 equal sides, but its angles are not all equal (130° and 100°), so it has only 2 lines of symmetry and order 2.

blocks.title: قاعدة المضلع المنتظم
blocks.text: المضلع المنتظم = كل الأضلاع متساوية وكل الزوايا متساوية. لو عنده n ضلع، يبقى عنده n محور تماثل، ورتبة التماثل الدوراني بتاعته n، وأصغر لفة بترجّعه زي ما كان = 360 ÷ n. القاعدة دي للمنتظم بس — المستطيل مثلاً 4 أضلاع لكن محورين بس.
6. Worked examples

**Worked example 1** [2 marks]
A quadrilateral has four equal sides. Its angles are 70°, 110°, 70° and 110°. Draw a ring around **every** name that is correct for this shape:
square     rhombus     rectangle     parallelogram     kite

items: Four equal sides but no right angles → it is a **rhombus**, not a square.
No right angles → it is not a rectangle.
Go up the hierarchy from rhombus: a rhombus is a **parallelogram** and a **kite**.
**Answer:** rhombus, parallelogram, kite. (2 marks for all three and no wrong ones; 1 mark for two correct and no wrong ones.)

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** ringing only 'rhombus'. The question says 'every name', so think about the hierarchy.

**Worked example 2** [3 marks]
Tick (✓) Correct or Not correct for each statement. If it is not correct, give a counter-example.
(a) Every square is a rhombus.  (b) Every rectangle is a square.  (c) Every rhombus is a parallelogram.

items: (a) **Correct.** A square has 4 equal sides and 2 pairs of parallel sides, so it has all the properties of a rhombus.
(b) **Not correct.** Counter-example: a rectangle 6 cm by 2 cm has right angles but its sides are not all equal, so it is not a square.
(c) **Correct.** A rhombus has two pairs of parallel sides, so it is a parallelogram.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 3** [2 marks]
The points A(1, 1), B(5, 1), C(6, 4) and D(2, 4) are joined in order. Write down the special name of ABCD. Give a reason.

blocks.caption: ABCD on a coordinate grid.

items: AB: 4 right, 0 up. DC: 4 right, 0 up. Same step → AB and DC are parallel and equal.
AD: 1 right, 3 up. BC: 1 right, 3 up. Same step → AD and BC are parallel and equal.
Two pairs of parallel sides → parallelogram family. AB = 4 but AD is a slanted side about 3.2 units long, so the sides are not all equal (not a rhombus). The angle at A is not 90° (not a rectangle).
**Answer:** a **parallelogram**, because both pairs of opposite sides are parallel (and equal) but there are no right angles and the sides are not all equal.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 4** [2 marks]
What am I? 'I am a quadrilateral. My diagonals are equal in length, they bisect each other and they cross at right angles.'

items: Diagonals equal and bisecting each other → rectangle family (rectangle or square).
Diagonals crossing at 90° and bisecting each other → rhombus family (rhombus or square).
The only shape in both families is the **square**.
**Answer:** square.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 5** [3 marks]
A regular polygon has rotational symmetry of order 12.
(a) How many lines of symmetry does it have? (b) How many sides does it have? (c) What is the smallest angle you can turn it through so that it looks the same?

items: (a) Regular polygon: lines of symmetry = order of rotation = **12**.
(b) Number of sides = **12** (a regular dodecagon).

blocks.text:
**Worked example 6** [1 mark]
A regular polygon looks exactly the same after a turn of 40° about its centre. How many sides does it have?
**Working:** the number of turns that make a full turn = 360° ÷ 40° = 9. **Answer: 9 sides** (a regular nonagon).

**Common mistake:** dividing 360 by the number of sides when the question gives the angle, or giving the angle when the question asks for the number of sides. Write the rule first: smallest turn = 360° ÷ n.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Saying 'a square is not a rectangle'. It is: it has 4 right angles and opposite sides equal and parallel.
Reading the hierarchy downwards: 'all rectangles are squares' or 'all parallelograms are rhombuses' are false.
Thinking a rectangle has 4 lines of symmetry. Its diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry: it has only 2.
Thinking a parallelogram has lines of symmetry. It has none, but it has rotational symmetry of order 2.
Using the n-lines rule for a shape that is not regular (rectangle, kite, a hexagon with equal sides but different angles).
Writing 'order 0' for no rotational symmetry. The lowest order is 1.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: "Draw a ring around the correct name(s)." Read whether it says one name or every name.
"Tick Correct or Not correct" for statements like 'every rhombus is a square'. If it is not correct, a counter-example is the strongest reason.
"Complete the table" of properties (sides, angles, diagonals, lines of symmetry, order of rotation).
Points on a coordinate grid: "What type of quadrilateral is ABCD?" or "Write the coordinates of D so that ABCD is a parallelogram."
Regular polygons: "A regular polygon has 9 lines of symmetry. Write down its order of rotational symmetry." One-mark facts: write the number, not a sentence.
Explain questions: use mathematical words such as parallel, perpendicular, adjacent, opposite, diagonal and bisect.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Quadrilaterals and regular polygons — practice
blocks.intro: 14 questions, from easy to Checkpoint-hard. Calculator not needed. Use the hierarchy diagram and the symmetry rule.

questions.q: Which quadrilateral **always** has diagonals that cross at right angles?
questions.e: The diagonals of a kite always cross at 90° (one of them bisects the other). A rectangle's diagonals are equal but do not usually cross at 90°; parallelograms and trapezia have no such rule.

questions.q: I am a quadrilateral. All four of my sides are equal, but none of my angles is a right angle. What is my special name?
questions.e: 4 equal sides → rhombus or square. No right angles → not a square. Answer: rhombus.

A square has two pairs of parallel sides, so it is always a parallelogram. The others are only sometimes true (a rectangle or rhombus is a square only when it has both equal sides and right angles; a kite is a parallelogram only when it is a rhombus).

questions.q: How many lines of symmetry does a regular octagon have?
questions.e: Regular polygon with 8 sides → 8 lines of symmetry.

questions.q: A regular polygon has rotational symmetry of order 15. How many sides does it have?
questions.e: For a regular polygon, order of rotational symmetry = number of sides = 15.

questions.q: A regular decagon has 10 sides. What is the smallest angle it can be turned through about its centre so that it looks exactly the same?
Which shape has **no** lines of symmetry but **has** rotational symmetry of order 2?
questions.e: A general parallelogram has 0 lines of symmetry but fits onto itself after a half turn (order 2). Kite: 1 line, order 1. Isosceles trapezium: 1 line, order 1. Rhombus: 2 lines, order 2.

questions.q: What is the special name of quadrilateral ABCD?
questions.e: AB: 2 right, 3 up; BC: 2 right, 3 down → AB = BC (mirror images in the line x = 3). DA: 2 left, 4 up; CD: 2 left, 4 down → AD = CD. Two pairs of adjacent equal sides, AB ≠ AD, and no parallel sides → kite. (Also: diagonal AC is horizontal and BD is vertical, so they cross at 90°, and BD bisects AC.)

questions.q: Explain why a square is a special type of rectangle.
questions.ms: 1 mark: a square has every property of a rectangle, e.g. 'it has 4 right angles and its opposite sides are equal and parallel' (and it also has all sides equal). Do not accept 'because it has 4 sides' alone.
questions.e: A rectangle is a quadrilateral with 4 right angles (so opposite sides are equal and parallel). A square has 4 right angles and opposite sides equal and parallel, so it has every property of a rectangle. It also has the extra property that all 4 sides are equal, which makes it a special rectangle.

questions.q: A regular polygon has 9 lines of symmetry. What is its order of rotational symmetry?
questions.e: Regular polygon: lines of symmetry = order of rotational symmetry = number of sides = 9.

questions.q: A quadrilateral is a parallelogram **and** a kite. Which special name must it have?
questions.e: A kite has two pairs of adjacent equal sides; a parallelogram has opposite sides equal. Together, all four sides are equal, so it is a rhombus. It does not have to have right angles, so it need not be a square.

questions.q: The diagonals of a quadrilateral are equal in length and bisect each other, but they do **not** cross at right angles. What is the special name of the quadrilateral?
questions.e: Equal diagonals that bisect each other → rectangle or square. Not at right angles → not a square. Answer: rectangle.

questions.q: A regular polygon looks exactly the same after a turn of 20° about its centre (20° is the smallest such turn). How many sides does it have?
questions.e: Smallest turn = 360° ÷ n, so n = 360° ÷ 20° = 18 sides. Check: 18 × 20° = 360°.

questions.p: Omar draws this hexagon. All six sides are 3 cm long.

questions.q: Omar says: 'My hexagon has 6 lines of symmetry because it has 6 equal sides.' Explain why Omar is wrong.
questions.ms: 1 mark: the hexagon is not regular / its angles are not all equal (equal sides are not enough). 1 mark: so the rule 'n sides → n lines' does not apply; it has only 2 lines of symmetry (accept 'fewer than 6').
questions.e: The rule 'n sides = n lines of symmetry' is only for regular polygons. A regular polygon needs equal sides AND equal angles. Omar's hexagon has angles of 130° and 100°, so it is not regular. It has only 2 lines of symmetry (one vertical and one horizontal through the centre) and rotational symmetry of order 2.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Learn the properties of the square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram, trapezium and kite: sides, angles, diagonals, symmetry.
A shape lower in the hierarchy has all the properties of the shapes above it: a square is a rectangle and a rhombus; a rhombus is a parallelogram and a kite.
The hierarchy does not work upside down. One counter-example proves a statement false.
A regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order n; the smallest turn is 360° ÷ n.
The rule is only for regular polygons (equal sides AND equal angles).
